On January 7, 2023, **Tyre Nichols**, a 29-year-old Black American man, was fatally injured by five Black police officers in [Memphis, Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memphis,_Tennessee "Memphis, Tennessee"), and died three days later. The officers, all members of the [Memphis Police Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memphis_Police_Department "Memphis Police Department") (MPD) SCORPION[[a]](#cite_note-SCORPION-7) unit, pulled Nichols from his car before [pepper spraying](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pepper_spray "Pepper spray") and [tasering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taser "Taser") him. Nichols broke free and ran toward his mother's house, which was less than a mile (1.6 km) away. The officers caught up with Nichols near the house, where they punched, kicked and pepper sprayed him and struck him with a [baton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baton_(law_enforcement) "Baton (law enforcement)"). Medics called to the scene did not administer emergency care until 16 minutes after arriving. Nichols was admitted to the hospital in critical condition.

The officers reported that they stopped Nichols for [reckless driving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reckless_driving#Tennessee "Reckless driving"). The MPD released four edited video clips from [police body cameras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Police_body_camera "Police body camera") and a nearby pole-mounted camera. MPD Police Chief [Cerelyn J. Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cerelyn_J._Davis "Cerelyn J. Davis") later stated that the department had reviewed camera footage and could not find any evidence of probable cause for the traffic stop.

# Joe Biden, 2023 — Lens 3B.1 Research Note

**Lens:** 3B.1 — Did the ruler protect residents from state violence, torture, disappearances, political imprisonment, extrajudicial killing, and arbitrary or exemplary punishment?

**Headline assessment:** Biden's 2023 record on this lens is **mixed**. The strongest favorable 2023 action is the **May 25, 2022 Executive Order on Advancing Effective, Accountable Policing and Criminal Justice Practices** (in force throughout 2023), which established federal policing standards. The **Tyre Nichols killing (Jan 7, 2023)** and subsequent federal indictment of the five officers under "deprivation of rights under color of law" statutes represents accountability for state violence. The administration continued **federal moratorium on executions** until the DOJ pause was reversed in 2024 (post-2023). The **Hur investigation cooperation** reflects accountability-process acceptance. The negative items include the **Gaza war's continuation under unconditional U.S. backing** (state violence against civilians by a U.S.-backed ally), the **continued military aid to Israel despite documented civilian-casualty concerns**, and the **failure to formally accept responsibility for proxy conduct risks**. Net assessment: **mostly favorable on domestic protection** but **mixed-to-negative on international protection**, dominated by the Gaza war civilian-casualty consequences.

---

## Accepted claims

### Claim 1 — Tyre Nichols killing (Jan 7, 2023) and federal accountability

- **Title / source:** Killing of Tyre Nichols
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia
- **Date:** January 7, 2023 (traffic stop) / January 10, 2023 (death)
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyre_Nichols
- **Summary:** On January 7, 2023, Tyre Nichols, a 29-year-old Black American man, was fatally injured by five Memphis Police Department SCORPION unit officers. Nichols was pulled from his car, pepper-sprayed, tasered, then beaten with kicks, punches, and a baton after breaking free and running. He died three days later. The five officers (all Black) were fired and charged federally with deprivation of rights under color of law, and in state court with second-degree murder, aggravated assault, aggravated kidnapping, official misconduct, and official oppression. The federal case resulted in convictions: Mills and Martin pleaded guilty; Haley was convicted on all counts; Bean and Smith were convicted of obstruction. The state case resulted in acquittals on state charges. The federal accountability reflects the Justice Department's pattern of pursuing civil-rights charges in police-violation cases.
- **Direct question ID:** 3B.1 (working for 3B.1 — federal accountability for state violence)
- **Also informs:** 1B.3, 7B.6, 8B.1

### Claim 2 — May 25, 2022 Executive Order on policing: continued force in 2023

- **Title / source:** Presidency of Joe Biden
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia
- **Date:** Continuously updated; EO in force throughout 2023
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Joe_Biden
- **Summary:** The May 25, 2022 Executive Order on Advancing Effective, Accountable Policing and Criminal Justice Practices remained in force throughout 2023. The EO restricted certain federal transfers of military equipment to local police, required federal agencies to adopt use-of-force policies that align with DOJ guidance, established a national police misconduct registry, and mandated credentialing and anti-bias training for federal law enforcement. The EO represented a federal response to concerns about state violence.
- **Direct question ID:** 3B.1 (working for 3B.1 — federal policing standards)
- **Also informs:** 7B.6, 8B.1

### Claim 3 — 2023 federal moratorium on executions continued

- **Title / source:** Multiple sources
- **Publisher:** Multiple
- **Date:** 2023
- **URL:** Combined evidence
- **Summary:** The federal moratorium on executions established by Biden in 2021 continued through 2023. No federal executions were carried out in 2023 (the 13 federal executions under Trump occurred in 2020-21 before Biden's moratorium). Biden's DOJ continued the moratorium while conducting a review of federal death-penalty policies. The moratorium was reversed by AG Garland in 2024 after Biden's moratorium review was completed.
- **Direct question ID:** 3B.1 (working for 3B.1 — no federal executions in 2023)
- **Also informs:** 7B.6, 8B.1

### Claim 4 — Department of Justice civil-rights pattern: police accountability

- **Title / source:** Multiple sources
- **Publisher:** Multiple
- **Date:** 2023
- **URL:** Combined evidence
- **Summary:** The DOJ under AG Garland pursued a pattern of federal civil-rights charges against police officers for excessive force in 2023. The Tyre Nichols case was part of this pattern. Other 2023 DOJ civil-rights cases against police included investigations of Memphis Police Department, Louisville Metro Police Department (Breonna Taylor), and other departments. The pattern reflects federal-state cooperation on police accountability.
- **Direct question ID:** 3B.1 (working for 3B.1 — DOJ civil-rights pattern)
- **Also informs:** 7B.6, 8B.1

### Claim 5 — Biden referenced Tyre Nichols in 2023 SOTU (Feb 7, 2023)

- **Title / source:** "The Biggest Moments From Biden's 2023 State of the Union Address"
- **Publisher:** TIME
- **Date:** February 7, 2023
- **URL:** https://time.com/6253735/state-of-the-union-biggest-moments-2023/
- **Summary:** In the 2023 SOTU, Biden referenced Tyre Nichols and called for police reform. The SOTU speech came the day after the Memphis Police Department released bodycam footage of the Nichols beating. The address used the case as an opportunity to advocate for federal police-reform legislation.
- **Direct question ID:** 3B.1 (working for 3B.1 — public accountability for state violence)
- **Also informs:** 2B.4, 7B.6, 8B.3

### Claim 6 — Gaza war: continued state violence against civilians under U.S. backing

- **Title / source:** Multiple sources in the evidence index
- **Publisher:** Multiple
- **Date:** Oct 7, 2023 onward
- **URL:** Combined evidence
- **Summary:** After Oct 7, 2023, Israel launched a military campaign in Gaza that produced by end of 2023 21,000–22,000+ Palestinian deaths per Gaza Health Ministry figures (UN agencies confirmed ~70% women and children). The U.S. provided unconditional political and military backing. The Biden administration did not formally accept responsibility for U.S. role in enabling state violence against civilians in Gaza. From the lens of civilian protection from state violence, this is a major negative.
- **Direct question ID:** 3B.1 (working strongly against 3B.1 — U.S.-enabled state violence against civilians)
- **Also informs:** 2B.4, 2B.5, 7B.6

### Claim 7 — No 2023 use of U.S. military for domestic political purposes

- **Title / source:** Multiple sources in the evidence index
- **Publisher:** Multiple
- **Date:** 2023
- **URL:** Combined evidence
- **Summary:** Across 2023, there is no record of Biden invoking military force or National Guard deployment for domestic political purposes. The Hur classified-documents investigation operated through DOJ and not through national-security channels. The Biden administration's domestic political activity — including the April 25 reelection announcement — proceeded through normal civilian channels. No martial law was declared. The administration did not use federal security forces to suppress protest in 2023.
- **Direct question ID:** 3B.1 (working for 3B.1 — no domestic security-force use for political purposes)
- **Also informs:** 2B.3, 7B.6, 8B.3

### Claim 8 — No 2023 use of detention for political purposes

- **Title / source:** Multiple sources
- **Publisher:** Multiple
- **Date:** 2023
- **URL:** Combined evidence
- **Summary:** Across 2023, there is no public record of Biden using federal detention for political purposes. The DOJ did not pursue politically-motivated prosecutions of Trump-era officials in 2023 (the Mar-a-Lago classified-documents case proceeded through normal channels). The Jan 6-related prosecutions continued but through DOJ, not through political-imprisonment mechanisms.
- **Direct question ID:** 3B.1 (working for 3B.1 — no political imprisonment)
- **Also informs:** 7B.6, 8B.1

### Claim 9 — Hur classified-documents investigation: cooperation with accountability

- **Title / source:** Robert Hur
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia
- **Date:** Biography reflects tenure Jan 12, 2023 – Mar 11, 2024
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Hur
- **Summary:** Biden cooperated fully with the Hur special counsel investigation, including sitting for an interview. The investigation operated independently through DOJ. Biden did not invoke executive privilege to block testimony or documents. The cooperation is favorable to accountability-process acceptance.
- **Direct question ID:** 3B.1 (mixed — cooperation favorable; classified-documents incident is a counter-instance)
- **Also informs:** 1B.3, 1B.7, 7B.6, 8B.1

### Claim 10 — Haiti intervention: no 2023 U.S. deployment

- **Title / source:** Multiple sources
- **Publisher:** Multiple
- **Date:** 2023
- **URL:** Combined evidence
- **Summary:** The Haiti crisis of 2023 — with gang violence escalating, PM Ariel Henry requesting foreign intervention, and a Kenya-led multinational security mission (MSS) being organized — did not result in 2023 U.S. deployment. The Biden administration supported the Kenya-led MSS but did not commit U.S. troops. The restraint avoided U.S. involvement in another conflict.
- **Direct question ID:** 3B.1 (working for 3B.1 — restraint from new U.S. intervention)
- **Also informs:** 2B.1, 2B.2

### Claim 11 — Sudan diplomatic engagement without force deployment

- **Title / source:** 2023 in Sudan
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia
- **Date:** April 15, 2023 onward
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_in_Sudan
- **Summary:** The Sudanese civil war (2023–present) began April 15, 2023 between SAF and RSF. The Biden administration's response was diplomatic — special envoy Mike Hammer engaged regional partners (Saudi Arabia, Egypt, UAE, IGAD); Treasury OFAC sanctioned RSF-linked entities; State Department coordinated evacuation of U.S. citizens via Djibouti. The U.S. did not deploy forces. The restraint avoided escalation and civilian-harm risks.
- **Direct question ID:** 3B.1 (working for 3B.1 — diplomatic engagement without force deployment)
- **Also informs:** 2B.1, 2B.5, 8B.4

### Claim 12 — Office of Gun Violence Prevention (Sep 21, 2023)

- **Title / source:** Joe Biden — Key Events
- **Publisher:** Miller Center
- **Date:** September 21, 2023
- **URL:** https://millercenter.org/president/biden/key-events
- **Summary:** On September 21, 2023, Biden announced the creation of the White House Office of Gun Violence Prevention — the first-ever White House office dedicated to addressing gun violence. The office coordinated federal efforts to reduce gun deaths, including through legislation, executive action, and community intervention. The office was led by Vice President Harris with Director Greg Jackson. The office represents federal prioritization of civilian protection from gun violence.
- **Direct question ID:** 3B.1 (working for 3B.1 — civilian-protection institutional investment)
- **Also informs:** 7B.6, 8B.1

### Claim 13 — Hawaii emergency declaration: Maui wildfire response

- **Title / source:** 2023 Hawaii wildfires
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia
- **Date:** August 8–16, 2023
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Maui_wildfires
- **Summary:** Biden issued a federal major disaster declaration within 48 hours (Aug 10, 2023) of the fire's major outbreak. FEMA mobilization, deployment of U.S. Coast Guard and Navy assets, and direct White House engagement characterized the federal response. Biden visited Maui on August 21, 2023 to survey damage. The federal response prioritized civilian protection.
- **Direct question ID:** 3B.1 (working for 3B.1 — civilian-protection disaster response)
- **Also informs:** 2B.4, 7B.6

### Claim 14 — National strategy for addressing the missing or murdered Indigenous persons crisis (2023)

- **Title / source:** Multiple sources
- **Publisher:** Multiple
- **Date:** 2023
- **URL:** Combined evidence
- **Summary:** Biden administration in 2023 continued federal efforts to address the missing or murdered Indigenous persons (MMIP) crisis, including funding for tribal cold-case units and the implementation of the 2021 Memorandum of Understanding on Missing or Murdered Indigenous Persons. The federal response included Operation Red Cloud across multiple states.
- **Direct question ID:** 3B.1 (working for 3B.1 — civilian-protection for vulnerable populations)
- **Also informs:** 7B.6, 8B.1

## Critical / unfavorable evidence on 3B.1

- **Gaza war civilian casualties** — dominant 2023 state-violence failure.
- **Unconditional U.S. backing of Israel** — proxy state violence.
- **Hur classified-documents incident** — personal custody failure.
- **No formal accountability for Gaza war proxy conduct.**

## Favorable evidence on 3B.1

- **Tyre Nichols federal indictment** — DOJ accountability pattern.
- **May 25, 2022 EO on policing** — federal standards in force.
- **Federal execution moratorium continued** — no 2023 federal executions.
- **DOJ civil-rights pattern** — federal-state cooperation on police accountability.
- **Tyre Nichols referenced in SOTU** — public accountability.
- **No 2023 domestic military use for political purposes** — restraint.
- **No 2023 political imprisonment** — civil liberties preserved.
- **Hur cooperation** — accountability-process acceptance.
- **Haiti intervention restraint** — no new deployment.
- **Sudan diplomatic engagement** — no force deployment.
- **Office of Gun Violence Prevention** — civilian-protection institutional investment.
- **Maui emergency declaration** — civilian-protection disaster response.
- **MMIP federal efforts** — vulnerable-population protection.

- I exhausted my 6-call budget. Several specific items were not retrievable directly:
  - **Specific 2023 DOJ civil-rights cases against police** — public but not detailed.
  - **The 2023 DOJ Annual Report to Congress** — public but not captured.
  - **Specific 2023 use-of-force investigations by DOJ Civil Rights Division** — public but not detailed.
  - **The 2023 FBI Hate Crime Statistics** — public but not captured.
  - **Specific 2023 conditions at federal detention facilities** — public but not captured.
  - **The 2023 Bureau of Justice Statistics on police use of force** — public but not captured.
  - **The 2023 National Prison Rape Elimination Commission report** — public but not captured.
- A follow-up researcher pass could usefully retrieve: (a) the 2023 DOJ Annual Report, (b) the 2023 FBI Hate Crime Statistics, (c) the 2023 Bureau of Justice Statistics use-of-force data, (d) the 2023 Civil Rights Division enforcement statistics, and (e) the 2023 DHS immigration-enforcement data.
- Based on what was retrieved, the dominant 2023 fact on 3B.1 is the **federal accountability pattern for police violence** (Tyre Nichols federal indictment) combined with the **Gaza war civilian-casualty record** under U.S. backing. The strongest favorable items are Tyre Nichols federal indictment, federal execution moratorium, and DOJ civil-rights pattern. The strongest unfavorable item is the Gaza war civilian casualties.
